1.meaning: A command addressed to a single person: 'Read!' or 'Recite!' — the very first word of the Qur'an to be revealed. It carries the sense of reciting aloud, proclaiming, and conveying, not merely reading silently from a page.

parts.en: helping vowel that begins the command (added because the verb root would otherwise start with a vowelless consonant)
read / recite (the command form of the verb); the closing apostrophe is the third root letter, the hamza (ء)

1.grammar: This is a command (imperative) verb directed at one male person ('you', singular). It has no person-prefix because Arabic commands are built directly from the verb; the opening i- is just a helper sound to make the word pronounceable. The verb has no object stated after it, which lets the command stand absolutely: simply 'Read!' / 'Recite!'
1.root: ق-ر-ء (q-r-ʾ) — to read, recite, gather words together; the same root that gives the word 'Qur'an'

2.meaning: 'In the name of' / 'with the name of' — invoking and beginning by means of a name. The phrase frames the act of reciting as something done in the name and by the authority of the One about to be mentioned.

parts.en: with / in / by means of (an attached preposition)

2.grammar: The little word bi- ('with/in') is glued to the front and forces the noun after it into the genitive case — that is why 'name' ends in -i (ismi) rather than -u. The -i ending also sets up a possessive link to the next word, giving 'name OF your Lord'. The alif at the start of ism stays in the written text; what drops is only the spoken glottal onset, so after bi- the two run together in pronunciation as bismi.
2.root: س-م-و (s-m-w) — height, a name (that by which something is raised up and known)

3.meaning: 'Your Lord' — Rabb means the Master, Owner, Sustainer and Nurturer who creates, provides for, and steadily brings His creation to its completion. It is far richer than 'lord' in English: the One who originates you and cares for every stage of your growth. Here it is 'your Lord', spoken to the Prophet.
3.grammar: The stem 'Rabb' shows the genitive -i ending (rabbi) because it is the second term of a possessive construct with the preceding 'name' (name OF your Lord). In this pairing 'name' is the thing possessed and 'Lord' is the possessor, and Arabic puts the possessor into the genitive. Attached at the end is -ka, the possessive pronoun 'your' for a single male — so the whole phrase means 'the name belonging to your Lord'.
3.root: ر-ب-ب (r-b-b) — to nurture, sustain, master, and bring something gradually to its full state

4.meaning: 'The One Who' / 'He Who' — a connecting word that points to a specific, known being and introduces a description of Him. Here it links 'your Lord' to what follows, telling us which Lord: the One who created.

parts.en: the one who / he who (masculine singular)

4.grammar: This is a relative pronoun ('the one who'), fixed in form for a single male and never changing its endings for case. It does the job of the English words 'who/which' by attaching a whole describing clause ('...who created') onto the noun before it, 'your Lord'.
4.root: — (a pronoun; it has no triliteral root)

5.meaning: 'He created' — He brought into existence, originated, and shaped from nothing. No object is mentioned, so the meaning is left open and all-embracing: He created everything that exists.

parts.en: he created / he brought into being

5.grammar: This is a past-tense verb meaning the action is complete: 'He created'. The final -a (khalaqa) is the standard ending of a simple past-tense verb for 'he', so no separate word for 'He' is needed — it is built into the verb. The verb is left without a stated object, which makes the creating absolute and universal.
5.root: خ-ل-ق (kh-l-q) — to create, originate, fashion, and proportion

1.meaning: He created — meaning Allah brought the human being into existence out of nothing, forming and originating it. The verb carries the sense of fashioning and bringing about something that did not exist before.
1.grammar: A past-tense verb in the third-person masculine singular: 'He created.' The subject 'He' (Allah) is not a separate ending — it is built into the verb and understood from the previous ayah (in this basic past form, 'he' is marked by the absence of any suffix). The whole word khalaqa is the verb stem on the faʿala (CaCaCa) pattern; its final -a is the stem's own vowel, and it marks completed action: the creating is done, not ongoing.
1.root: خ-ل-ق (kh-l-q) — to create, originate, fashion out of nothing

2.meaning: The human being / mankind — humankind as a species, the creature Allah singles out here as the noblest of His creation. The 'al-' makes it general, pointing to humanity as a whole rather than one specific person.
2.grammar: A noun with the definite article 'al-' ('the'), used here for the whole class — 'humankind.' Its final -a (al-insāna) is the accusative case ending, which marks it as the direct object of the verb: it is the thing being created — '(He) created the human being.'
2.root: أ-ن-س (ʾ-n-s) — to be sociable, familiar, companionable; the human as a social being

3.meaning: From — a particle showing the starting point or raw material out of which something is made. Here it marks the origin of the human being: the substance creation began from.
3.grammar: A preposition meaning 'from' or 'out of.' It does not change its form. It introduces the source material of the creation and puts the word after it into the genitive case (hence the -in ending on the next word).

4.meaning: A clinging clot — a small mass of congealed or clotted blood that clings and attaches itself (to the wall of the womb). The word evokes something that hangs on and adheres, describing the lowly, humble origin from which Allah brings forth the honoured human being.
4.grammar: An indefinite noun, 'a clinging clot.' The final -in ending (ʿalaqin) is the genitive case with tanwīn (nunation) — the -n sound signals 'a/some' (indefinite), and the -i part is required because it follows the preposition 'min' ('from'). Together: 'from a clinging clot.'
4.root: ع-ل-ق (ʿ-l-q) — to cling, hang, attach; hence a clot that clings

1.meaning: A command meaning 'Read!' or 'Recite!' It is the same opening word as in verse 1, addressed to the Prophet. Here it carries the sense of proclaiming and conveying aloud what is revealed, not silent reading.

parts.en: helping vowel that begins the command form
read / recite (the final ' is the hamza, the third root letter)

1.grammar: This is a direct command (imperative) to a single male listener: 'you, read!' It is built from the past-tense verb qara'a ('he read'), whose three root letters are q, r and the hamza (a glottal catch). That hamza is the actual final sound of the word — written as a small seated mark after the alif and heard as the apostrophe in 'iq'ra'. The command form takes no extra vowel or pronoun on the end, which is what marks it as an order to one person; the initial i- is just a helper sound Arabic adds because the root would otherwise begin with two unvoweled letters.
1.root: ق-ر-ء (q-r-ʾ) — to read, recite, gather words together

2.meaning: 'And your Lord' — referring to Allah as the One who creates, owns, sustains, nurtures and brings every creature to its completion. 'Lord' (rabb) bundles together the ideas of master, provider and caring upbringer; it is far richer than merely a title of rank.
2.grammar: The wa- prefix means 'and'. The word rabb takes the -u ending, which marks it as the subject/topic of the sentence: 'your Lord IS...' — it sets up the statement completed by the next word. The attached -ka means 'your', addressed to a single male (the Prophet), and shows possession: this Lord belongs to / cares for you.
2.root: ر-ب-ب (r-b-b) — to nurture, master, sustain and bring to completion

3.meaning: 'The Most Generous' — the One whose giving is boundless and unmatched, who bestows favours freely without being asked and without seeking any benefit in return. It conveys the very highest, most noble form of generosity and honour.
3.grammar: The al- prefix means 'the', making it definite and singling Allah out uniquely. The word akram is a superlative pattern (af'al) meaning 'most generous of all', and its -u ending matches 'your Lord' from the previous word — together they read 'your Lord IS the Most Generous', completing the sentence's statement about Him.

1.meaning: A relative pronoun meaning "the One Who" or "He Who." It refers back to "your Lord" (rabbuka) in the previous verse and introduces a new description of Him: it is Allah who is about to be described as the One who taught by the pen.
1.grammar: A masculine singular relative pronoun ("the one who"). It is a fixed, indeclinable word, so its ending never changes for case. Here it functions as a further description of "your Lord" from the previous verse, linking Him to the action that follows ("...who taught by the pen").

2.meaning: "He taught" or "He instructed" — to impart knowledge to someone. The doubled middle letter gives an intensive, thorough sense: He fully and deliberately conveyed knowledge, not merely passed it along. The subject is Allah, carried over from the previous verse.
2.grammar: A past-tense verb, form II, built on the pattern faʿʿala (note the doubled middle root letter, the "ll"). This doubling makes the basic root "to know" causative/intensive — "to cause to know," i.e. "to teach." It is third person masculine singular ("He taught"); in the past tense this person/gender/number is the default unmarked form and carries no suffix. The fatḥah (-a) on the final letter is simply the stem vowel sitting on the last root letter م, not a subject ending. The subject is Allah.

3.meaning: "By means of the pen" — through the instrument of writing. The pen stands for written knowledge: Allah taught humankind to record and transmit what they know, preserving learning across generations.
3.grammar: A prefixed preposition bi- ("by/with, by means of") attached to "the pen." A preposition forces the noun after it into the genitive case, which is why the word ends in -i (qalam-i) rather than -u; the -i here simply shows it is governed by "by." The al- is the definite article "the."
3.root: ق-ل-م (q-l-m) — to cut/trim (a reed); hence the pen (a trimmed reed)

1.meaning: He taught — and specifically taught thoroughly, repeatedly, with care, until knowledge was firmly transmitted. The doubled middle letter intensifies the plain verb 'to know,' turning 'He knew' into 'He caused (someone) to know,' i.e. He instructed and imparted knowledge. The subject is Allah; the verse celebrates Him as the ultimate Teacher of humankind.

parts.en: He taught / instructed (with the doubled middle letter giving the sense of thorough, deliberate teaching)

1.grammar: A past-tense verb, third-person masculine singular: 'He taught.' It is Form II (the middle root letter is doubled, shown by the shadda), which turns the basic verb 'to know' into a causative/intensive 'to make known, to teach.' The final -a vowel is simply the ordinary ending of this past-tense form; there is no attached pronoun, and the doer ('He,' i.e. Allah) is carried inside the verb itself.

2.meaning: Humankind; the human being as a species. Here it is used collectively for all of humanity — the creature Allah singled out to receive knowledge. Classical lexicographers trace the word to two competing roots: one (ʾ-n-s) linked to being sociable, familiar, and at ease with others, and another (n-s-y) linked to forgetfulness — fitting the human tendency to forget. Both derivations are well attested and neither is decisively established over the other.

parts.en: the (definite article; here it points to humankind as a whole / as a kind)

2.grammar: A noun with the definite article 'al-' ('the human being / mankind'). The 'a' of al- is not pronounced after the preceding word, so it reads 'l-insāna.' It is the direct object of the verb 'taught,' which is why it ends in -a (the accusative case): it is the one being taught. Although singular in form, it is meant generically — humanity as a whole.
2.root: Two derivations are recorded: أ-ن-س (ʾ-n-s) — being sociable, familiar; or ن-س-ي (n-s-y) — forgetting. Classical sources (e.g. Ibn Fāris, Lisān al-ʿArab) note both without settling the question.

3.meaning: 'That which' / 'what.' A connecting word that introduces the thing taught: it stands in for the content of the teaching — namely, the knowledge that humans did not previously possess. It functions like English 'what' in 'what he did not know.'
3.grammar: A relative pronoun, 'what / that which.' It is invariable — it never changes its ending for case, gender, or number. Grammatically it serves as the second object of 'taught' (Allah taught the human being [object 1] that-which [object 2]...), and it opens the clause that the following words complete. The long -ā is part of the word itself, not a case ending.

4.meaning: A negating word meaning 'did not.' It cancels the action of the verb that follows and pushes its meaning into the past: paired with the verb 'know,' it yields 'did not know.' It is a precise tool for stating that something definitely did not happen in the past.

parts.en: did not (negates the following verb and places it in the past)

4.grammar: A negative particle that governs the verb after it. Although it carries a past meaning ('did not'), it is followed by the present/imperfect verb form and forces a special ending on it called the jussive — which is why the next word loses its final vowel and ends in a silent stop (yaʿlam, not yaʿlamu). 'lam' itself never changes; its own final consonant is silent here (sukūn).

5.meaning: 'He knew' / 'he had knowledge of.' Here, governed by the preceding negator, it means 'he did not know.' The picture is of the knowledge humankind lacked before Allah granted it — the realm of understanding a person has no access to until it is taught.

parts.en: he knows / (under the preceding 'lam') he knew

5.grammar: A present/imperfect verb, third-person masculine singular, from the basic Form I 'to know.' The 'ya-' prefix marks the doer as 'he.' Normally this form would end in -u (yaʿlamu), but because the negator 'lam' precedes it, the ending is cut off to a silent stop (sukūn): yaʿlam. That clipped ending is the grammatical signal that 'lam' has turned it into a completed past negation: 'he did not know.' The subject 'he' refers back to the human being.

1.meaning: A sharp word of rebuke and restraint meaning 'No! Not at all!' It firmly checks and rejects the wrong attitude that follows — humanity's ingratitude after Allah has so generously created and taught him. It can also carry the sense 'Truly, indeed,' arresting the listener's attention before a solemn statement.
1.grammar: An indeclinable particle of deterrence and rebuke — it has no case ending and never changes form. The doubled 'l' (shown by the shadda) intensifies it, giving the force of an emphatic, final 'Absolutely not.' It stands alone, cutting off the preceding thought and bracing the listener for what comes next.

2.meaning: An emphasis particle placed at the head of a sentence to stress and certify what follows, roughly 'Indeed,' 'Truly,' or 'Most certainly.' It does not translate as a single English word; rather it solemnly assures the hearer that the statement to come is firmly established and true.
2.grammar: An emphatic particle (one of the 'sisters of inna') that governs the noun after it: it puts that noun — here al-insān — into the accusative case, which is why it appears as 'al-insāna' with a final '-a'. Inna itself is indeclinable and takes no ending. Think of it as underlining the whole sentence: 'It is genuinely the case that…'

3.meaning: Humankind, the human being — mankind considered as a species, here highlighting his characteristic forgetfulness and tendency to overreach once he feels self-sufficient.
3.grammar: A definite noun: the prefix 'al-' ('the') makes it specific, and here it denotes the whole human race (the generic 'the human being'). The final '-a' ending is accusative case (naṣb): it is the 'ism inna' (the noun governed by inna). Inna and its sisters take the noun that would otherwise be the nominative subject (mubtada) and pull it into the accusative, so grammatically it is now classified as the ism inna rather than the subject — 'indeed, the human being…'. The hamza-carrying 'i' opens the word; the long 'ā' sits in the second syllable.
3.root: أ-ن-س (ʾ-n-s) — to be familiar, sociable, humankind

4.meaning: He surely transgresses — he oversteps all proper limits, rebels, and becomes tyrannical and arrogant. The verb pictures someone exceeding the bounds set by Allah, swelling beyond what is right once he imagines himself beyond need.
4.grammar: Two pieces. The prefix 'la-' is the 'lām of emphasis' that regularly pairs with 'inna' — together they make the assertion doubly strong ('indeed… he surely does'). The verb 'yaṭghā' is present-tense, third-person masculine singular ('he transgresses'), the 'ya-' prefix marking 'he.' Its final long '-ā' (a defective/weak final root letter written as alif maqṣūra) is the verb's natural ending; being emphasised by 'la-', it stays in the indicative, conveying an ongoing, habitual overstepping — 'he keeps transgressing.'
4.root: ط-غ-ي (ṭ-gh-y) — to overflow, exceed all bounds, tyrannize

1.meaning: A linking particle meaning roughly "that" or "because." Here it introduces the reason for man's rebellion described in the previous verse: man transgresses BECAUSE / on account of the fact THAT he regards himself as needing no one. It turns the clause that follows into the cause or grounds of that arrogance.
1.grammar: A subordinating particle (here the "an" that means "because of the fact that"). It is indeclinable, so it has no case ending of its own; the silent ending (sukun on the n) is fixed and never changes. Its job is purely to connect: it makes the verb after it ("he sees himself…") into the explanation for why man rebels.

2.meaning: "He sees / considers himself." The verb is the perception verb "to see," used here in the sense of "to deem, to regard, to consider oneself to be." The attached "him(self)" makes man both the one seeing and the one seen: he views his own self as something — namely, as not needing anyone.
2.grammar: A past-tense (perfect) verb, third-person masculine singular: the built-in subject is "he" (referring to "man" from the previous verse). The root's third (final) radical is the weak letter ya (ي); in the past tense it surfaces as the final long "-ā" (alif maqsura) — that is the "he saw" ending, not the middle radical. The ending "-hu" is an attached object pronoun, "him" — since the seer and the seen are the same person, it carries the sense "himself." Past tense here states a settled fact about man's outlook rather than a one-time past event.

3.meaning: "He has become self-sufficient / free of need." The idea is that man imagines he is rich enough, strong enough, and independent enough to require nothing — not wealth from others and, by implication, not his Lord. It is the false sense of self-reliance that breeds arrogance.

parts.en: sought / considered oneself to be (form X prefix)

3.grammar: A past-tense (perfect) verb, third-person masculine singular ("he…"), in the derived pattern Form X (the "ist-/ista-" pattern), which here carries the sense "to regard oneself as" or "to find oneself to be" — so "he deemed himself free of need, self-sufficient." The final long "-ā" is the weak last root letter appearing at the end of the past-tense verb. It has no subject pronoun attached; the "he" is built into the verb form and refers back to "man."
3.root: غ-ن-ي (gh-n-y) — richness, freedom from need, sufficiency

1.meaning: An emphatic opening particle, roughly 'Truly' or 'Most certainly.' It has no clean English word of its own; its job is to stamp the whole sentence that follows with certainty and weight, assuring the listener that what comes next is an established, undeniable truth.
1.grammar: This is one of the 'sisters of inna' — a particle that governs the noun-sentence after it. It puts its subject (its ism) into the accusative case and adds strong emphasis, like saying 'It is absolutely the case that...'. It is a fixed particle, so it has no root, tense, or person of its own; the doubled n (shaddah) is simply part of the word.

2.meaning: A preposition meaning 'to,' 'toward,' or 'unto' — marking the end-point or destination of a movement or process. Here it points to the final destination to which everything ultimately heads back.
2.grammar: A genitive preposition: it forces the noun after it (rabbika, 'your Lord') into the genitive case. The dagger-alif ending (the small vertical stroke writing a long 'ā') is fixed — prepositions do not change for case, tense, or person. A preposition always precedes its object, so ilā coming before rabbika is just ordinary syntax and carries no special stress by itself. The emphasis in the verse comes instead from placing the whole prepositional phrase ilā rabbika (the predicate) ahead of the ism of inna (al-rujʿā), which puts the spotlight on the destination: 'to your Lord (and to none else).'

3.meaning: 'Your Lord' — the Master, Owner, Sustainer and Nurturer who creates, provides for, and brings each thing to its full completion. 'Rabb' is far richer than the English 'lord': it bundles together ownership, authority, care, and the act of raising something stage by stage to maturity. The attached 'your' addresses the Prophet (and every listener) directly and intimately.
3.grammar: The noun 'rabb' carries the genitive ending -i (rabbi). Its case is assigned solely by the preposition ilā in front of it — that is the only thing making it genitive here. The suffix -ka is an attached possessive pronoun meaning 'your,' addressed to a single male listener, and it makes the phrase a possessive construction (idāfa: 'the Lord OF you'), with rabb as the first term (muḍāf) and -ka as the second. Being the muḍāf does not by itself give a word any particular case; a muḍāf takes whatever case its role in the larger sentence demands, and here that role is 'object of ilā,' hence genitive. Note the word order: the phrase 'to your Lord' is placed before the subject, which in Arabic stresses that the return is to Him specifically.
3.root: ر-ب-ب (r-b-b) — to nurture, own, master, and sustain

4.meaning: 'The return' — the ultimate going-back, the final homecoming of all creation to Allah for reckoning. It names not a single trip but the great, certain return of everything to its Lord. This is the noun governed by inna (its ism), the thing the sentence asserts about: 'the return is to your Lord.'
4.grammar: This is the ism of inna, and as such it is in the accusative case — that is the defining effect of inna and its sisters on their subject. The accusative vowel is not heard or written here, however, because the word ends in a fixed long -ā (alif maqṣūra, written with a dagger-alif over yā), an invariable ending that stays the same in all three cases; so the accusative is grammatical but concealed, shown by inna's governance rather than by a visible vowel. The article al- makes it definite ('the return'); after the 'sun letter' r, the 'l' of al- assimilates into the r, which is why it is pronounced ar-rujʿā with a doubled r. The word is a feminine verbal noun on the pattern fuʿlā. Because inna's predicate (ilā rabbika) is fronted, this ism comes last in the verse, which heightens the sense of finality.
4.root: ر-ج-ع (r-j-ʿ) — to return, go back, come back

1.meaning: "Have you seen…?" or "Have you considered…?" — a rhetorical, attention-arresting question. It does not ask for information but invites the listener to reflect on and marvel at the outrageous person about to be described. Often it carries the sense "Tell Me about" or "Consider the case of…".

parts.en: perfect verb base "saw / considered" (the verb minus its subject suffix)

1.grammar: A past-tense (perfect) verb "you saw" with the interrogative hamza (a-) fused onto its front, turning the statement into the question "have you seen?". The middle segment رَءَيۡ is the body of the verb left after removing the prefix a- and before the subject suffix -ta — it is not the dictionary stem itself (the canonical Form I perfect 3rd-person-masculine stem is رَأَى, ra-ā). The final -ta ending marks the subject as "you" (one male) and shows the action is completed (perfect). Here the perfect is used rhetorically: the meaning is timeless — "consider this person" — rather than a literal past glance.

2.meaning: "The one who…" — a relative pronoun that points to a specific, known individual and links him to the action that follows. It singles out a particular man (traditionally understood as Abū Jahl) without naming him, setting up the description in the next word.
2.grammar: A relative pronoun, masculine singular, meaning "the (male) one who". It does not change for case here; its job is to connect the person just referred to ("have you seen…") with the clause that defines him ("who forbids…"). It functions as the object of "have you seen".

3.meaning: "…forbids" or "prohibits / tries to prevent" — the act of warning someone off, holding them back, and barring them from doing something. In context it describes a man who actively stops another from praying, so it conveys hostile prevention, not gentle advice.

parts.en: forbid / hold back (the two sound root letters n–h)
third (weak) root letter realized as the single long ā ending

3.grammar: A present/ongoing-tense (imperfect) verb, read yanhā with ONE long ā at the end. The ya- prefix means the subject is "he". The action is imperfect — habitual and ongoing — so it portrays the man as someone who keeps on forbidding. The ending is a single /ā/ sound: in the script the dagger alif (ٰ) over هـ supplies the vowel, while the alif maqṣūra ى is the verb's weak third root-letter (originally yāʾ) standing in final position; together they spell one long ā, the natural ending of such "defective" verbs in the present indicative.

1.meaning: A servant or worshipper — a person in humble bondage and devotion to Allah. Here it refers to a believing servant of Allah (understood to be the Prophet himself) whom the arrogant man tries to stop from praying. The word carries the sense of one who willingly submits and serves.

parts.en: accusative ending ('a servant', as the object)

1.grammar: A masculine singular noun, indefinite ('a servant', not 'the servant'). The final -an (tanwīn fatḥah) is the accusative case: it marks this word as the direct object of the verb 'forbids/prevents' back in the previous ayah — the arrogant man forbids 'a servant'. The indefiniteness also subtly magnifies the outrage: he would stop even a mere servant of Allah from worship.
1.root: ع-ب-د (ʿ-b-d) — to serve, worship, submit in devotion

2.meaning: A time-word meaning 'when' or 'whenever'. It introduces a circumstance and points to the moment an action takes place — here, the moment the servant stands in prayer. It frames 'praying' as the very situation in which the wrongdoer interferes.
2.grammar: An indeclinable adverb of time — it never changes its ending, so there is no case to read. It sets up a 'when…' clause and is normally followed by a verb describing what happens at that time (here, 'he prays'). It carries a sense of 'at the very moment that', highlighting the act of prayer as the trigger for the man's hostility.

3.meaning: He prayed / he performs the prayer — to carry out the formal act of worship (ṣalāh), with its standing, bowing, and prostration before Allah. The act being obstructed is this very devotion.

parts.en: to pray, perform the ritual prayer

3.grammar: A past-tense (perfect) verb, 'he prayed', third person masculine singular ('he'). It is Form II (the doubled middle root letter, ṣall-), the intensive/dedicated form that here names the established act of ritual prayer. After the time-word 'when', this past-tense verb carries a habitual sense — 'whenever he prays'. The final -ā is the verb's bare 3rd-person-masculine ending (the root's last weak letter appears as a long ā here, written with alif maqṣūra), with no extra suffix attached.
3.root: ص-ل-و / ص-ل-ي (ṣ-l-w/y) — prayer, ritual worship; supplication

1.meaning: "Have you considered?" / "Tell me—have you seen?" This is a rhetorical challenge addressed to a single male listener (the one who forbids the believer from praying, mentioned just before). It is not asking for literal eyesight; it invites the hearer to stop and reflect on a situation that is about to be described.
1.grammar: A past-tense verb carrying a built-in subject plus a question marker. The opening 'a-' turns the statement into a question. The stem 'ra-ʾay' is past tense ("saw"). The final '-ta' is the attached subject ending that means "you" (one male). Together with the 'a-' it reads "Have you seen / considered?" Here "seeing" is used in the sense of mentally considering, so the force is "What do you think about…?"
1.root: ر-أ-ي (r-ʾ-y) — to see, to perceive, to consider

2.meaning: "if" — a conditional particle that sets up a hypothetical case: it opens an "if… (then…)" structure, asking the listener to imagine a possibility before the consequence is weighed.
2.grammar: A conditional particle (an indeclinable function word, so it has no case ending and never changes form). It introduces the condition of an "if/then" sentence. Its answering clause is left unstated here for rhetorical effect, which is common in the Qur'an: the hearer is left to supply "…how serious is what he does!"

3.meaning: "he was / he is" — the past-tense verb "to be." Applied to a settled state like being guided, Arabic naturally uses this past form to mean "he is (in fact) upon…," describing the person's actual standing rather than a one-time past event.
3.grammar: The hollow verb "to be" in the past tense, third-person singular masculine: "he was." Its subject "he" is built in (referring to the servant who is being prevented from prayer). The final '-a' is the normal past-tense ending. After the conditional 'in' ("if"), it carries the sense "if he is / should he be." As "kāna" of being, it needs a following phrase to complete the meaning—supplied here by "upon guidance."
3.root: ك-و-ن (k-w-n) — to be, to exist, to come to be

4.meaning: "upon / on / following" — a preposition picturing being firmly set on top of something, here used figuratively for steadfastly adhering to and standing on the path of right guidance.
4.grammar: A preposition (a fixed function word). It governs the noun that follows it, putting that noun in the genitive (object-of-preposition) state. The image is of resting or standing "on" something; with guidance it conveys being solidly grounded in it. It links "he is" to its completion: "he is upon [guidance]."

5.meaning: "the (right) guidance" — the specific, true guidance from Allah: being shown and kept on the straight path of faith and obedience. The definite article marks it as THE guidance, not just any direction.
5.grammar: A definite noun: "the guidance." The prefix 'al-' is "the." Because it follows the preposition 'ʿalā' ("upon"), it is the object of that preposition and so is genitive; but its ending does not visibly change here because this word ends in a fixed long 'ā' (written on a yāʾ, هُدٰى) that stays the same in every case. So the case is genitive in function, shown by position rather than a new vowel. The phrase "upon the guidance" completes the condition: "…if he is upon [right] guidance."
5.root: ه-د-ي (h-d-y) — to guide, to show the right way

1.meaning: A connecting particle meaning "or" / "or else." Here it links this clause to the previous verse, offering a second possibility about the believer at prayer: that beyond being rightly guided himself (verse 11), he might also be calling others to do good. It presents an alternative, equally praiseworthy scenario.
1.grammar: An indeclinable particle of disjunction (it never changes form and takes no case ending). It coordinates two possibilities — "…if he is guided, OR if he enjoined righteousness" — joining this verse's verb to the conditional that began in the previous verse.

2.meaning: "He commanded / enjoined / urged" — to instruct or call someone to do something, here in the sense of bidding people toward what is good. The reference is to the believer who not only prays but also directs others to piety.
2.grammar: A past-tense (perfect) verb, third-person masculine singular: "he commanded." It is the bare Form I pattern (faʿala), with the final -a marking the completed past for a single male subject ("he"). Grammatically it falls under the "if" (in) of the previous verse, so the sense is "…or if he enjoined." What is commanded is introduced by the preposition bi- on the following word (the standard construction amara bi-).

3.meaning: "To/toward God-consciousness." Taqwā is a loaded term with no single English equivalent: it is the believer's protective God-consciousness — a vigilant awareness of Allah that guards a person from wrongdoing and moves them toward obedience, often rendered "piety" or "righteousness." The phrase means urging people toward this reverent mindfulness of Allah.
3.grammar: Built from the preposition bi- ("with/to") plus the definite article al- plus the noun taqwā. With the verb amara, bi- marks the object of the command — "commanded TO/WITH righteousness," i.e. enjoined it. The noun ends in a fixed alif maqṣūra (-ā); because this ending cannot carry a vowel, its genitive case after the preposition is implied (muqaddara) rather than pronounced. The sun-letter t assimilates the l of al- and doubles, giving "at-taqwā."
3.root: و-ق-ي (w-q-y) — to guard, shield, protect (whence taqwā: guarding oneself through God-consciousness)

1.meaning: "Have you considered / have you seen?" A rhetorical question that does not really seek information; it is used to make the listener stop and ponder a striking case — here, the man who forbids prayer. It carries the force of "Just look at / tell me about" the person being described.
1.grammar: Built on a past-tense verb "to see/consider." The opening اَ is the interrogative particle (hamzat al-istifham) — an independent particle merely written joined to the verb, turning the statement into a question ("have you…?"). The verb stem رَأَيۡ keeps the hamza (the glottal stop heard in raʾay). The final -ta is the attached subject ending meaning "you" (one male), so the form literally reads "have you seen?" In context it works as a rhetorical "just consider…," inviting reflection rather than a yes/no answer.

2.meaning: A conditional particle meaning "if" — it sets up a hypothetical or supposed case ("if it be that he denies…"), leaving the outcome to be drawn out. It does not by itself assert that the thing happened; it frames what follows as a supposition.
2.grammar: An indeclinable particle (it never changes form and has no case ending). It introduces a condition and governs the verbs after it, presenting the denial and turning-away as a supposed scenario being held up for thought.

3.meaning: "He cried lies / he denied (the truth)." More than a simple "he said no": it is to actively reject something as false — to brand the Messenger, the revelation, or the reckoning a lie and treat it as untrue.

parts.en: he denied / branded as a lie

3.grammar: A past-tense verb in the intensive (doubled-middle, Form II) pattern, which here makes it transitive and emphatic: not merely "to lie" but "to declare/treat as a lie." The doubling sits on the middle radical (the shaddah on ذّ), so it is correctly romanized "kadhdhaba"; note the source JSON's romanization "kadhaba" drops this gemination and so understates the Form II shape. The bare ending with a final -a and no added subject letters marks it as "he" (third person masculine singular) — "he denied." Standing after "if," it states the first half of the supposed case.
3.root: ك-ذ-ب (k-dh-b) — lying, falsehood, denying as untrue

4.meaning: "And he turned away / turned his back." To deliberately avert oneself — to reject and walk away from the truth or from obedience, not out of ignorance but as a turning of the back on guidance.

parts.en: he turned away / turned his back

4.grammar: Begins with the joining word wa- ("and"), linking it to the previous verb. The stem is a past-tense reflexive (Form V, ta- pattern) built on the idea of "turning," giving "to turn oneself away." It ends in a long final -ā (a weak-final verb) and carries no extra subject letters, so it means "he" (third masculine singular) — "and he turned away," completing the supposed case begun after "if."
4.root: و-ل-ي (w-l-y) — turning, being near/in charge; here turning away

1.meaning: A rhetorical 'Does he not...?' — not a real question seeking information but a rebuke aimed at the arrogant person of the previous verses, implying he certainly should know. It also fixes the negation in the past/perfect: 'Has he not (come to) know...?'
1.grammar: Two particles fused. The opening alif here carries the interrogative hamza (hamzat al-istifham, 'a-'), which turns the sentence into a question — here a rhetorical one expecting agreement. In this Uthmani spelling it is written as a plain alif rather than with a hamza sign, but it is read as the question particle. 'lam' is a special negative used before a present-tense verb: it both negates it and shifts its meaning into the past, so 'lam yaʿlam' = 'he did not / has not come to know.' 'lam' also forces the verb after it into the jussive form (see next word).

2.meaning: To know, to be aware of, to have certain knowledge of something. Here: for the human being to truly realize and take to heart a fact about Allah.
2.grammar: A present-tense verb, 3rd person masculine singular: the 'ya-' prefix means 'he.' The base form would be 'yaʿlamu' with a final '-u', but because the particle 'lam' comes before it, the verb is in the jussive mood — its final vowel is dropped to a silent ending (sukūn), giving 'yaʿlam'. This clipped ending is the grammatical sign that 'lam' is governing it.

3.meaning: 'that...indeed' — it opens the statement of what should be known, and at the same time stresses it as a firm, certain fact. The attached 'bi-' links this whole clause to the verb 'know' (i.e. 'know OF / ABOUT the fact that...').
3.grammar: A preposition plus an emphatic particle. 'bi-' ('of/about') connects the following content to the verb 'know.' 'anna' means 'that' and introduces a reported fact, but it carries built-in emphasis ('that...assuredly'). 'anna' belongs to the inna-family of particles, which govern the clause after them in a fixed way: the noun they take as their subject (the ism) goes into the accusative case, while the predicate (the khabar) stays in the nominative. That is why the next word, Allah, the ism of 'anna,' takes the accusative '-a' ending.

4.meaning: Allah — the proper name of the One God. Here named as the One whose all-seeing awareness the arrogant person has forgotten.
4.grammar: The proper name Allah, carrying the final '-a' (accusative) ending: 'Allāha.' That '-a' is required because it is the ism (subject) of the emphatic particle 'anna' just before it, and 'anna' puts its ism into the accusative case. In the meaning of the sentence Allah is the one who sees — 'that Allah sees' — even though the grammar marks the name with the accusative because of 'anna.'

5.meaning: He sees — He perceives and watches everything. The phrasing is open-ended ('sees'), so it sweeps in all things: every deed of the human being lies under Allah's gaze. A warning that nothing is hidden from Him.
5.grammar: A present-tense verb, 3rd person masculine singular: the 'ya-' prefix means 'He.' The root is ر-أ-ي, whose final letter is the consonant yā' (a 'weak' or defective root). In the present tense this final yā' undergoes a sound change and surfaces as a long '-ā' (written with alif maqsūra, ى), so the verb ends in 'yarā' rather than on a hard consonant — the root letter itself is a consonant, not a vowel. The present tense gives an ongoing, ever-true sense: 'He sees / is ever-seeing.' No object is stated, which leaves it general — He sees all.

1.meaning: A sharp word of rebuke and restraint meaning roughly 'No indeed! Stop that!' It does not negate a specific thing so much as forcefully reject the arrogant behaviour just described and warn the wrongdoer to halt. Often rendered 'Nay!' or 'But no!'
1.grammar: A standalone particle of deterrence and rejection (it does not take case endings). The doubled 'l' (shadda) gives it weight and finality, like a verbal slamming of the door. It functions as an exclamation that scolds and warns at once, setting up the threat that follows.

2.meaning: A two-part opener that sets up a solemn conditional: 'and surely, if…'. It primes the listener for a serious warning whose consequence is being sworn to.
2.grammar: Two joined particles. The prefixed lām (la-) is the 'lām of the oath', signalling that what comes is being emphatically affirmed, almost sworn. The stem 'in' is the conditional 'if', which introduces a hypothetical: it pairs with the later answering clause to mean 'if X happens, then surely Y'. Together they mean 'and truly, if…'.

3.meaning: A negating particle that turns the verb after it into a past-tense negative: 'did not' / 'has not'. Here it sets up 'has not desisted'.
3.grammar: A negation particle that governs the present-tense verb after it but flips its meaning into the negated past ('he does not / has not…'). Grammatically it puts that verb into the jussive mood, which is why the following verb loses its final vowel and is clipped (yantahī becomes yantahi). It negates completion: the act of stopping has not occurred.

4.meaning: 'He desists / stops / refrains' — i.e. he holds himself back from the arrogance and the forbidding of prayer mentioned earlier. With the preceding 'lam' the sense is 'if he does not desist'.

parts.en: desist / refrain (Form VIII stem of root n-h-y)

4.grammar: A present/future verb, third-person masculine singular ('he'), built on Form VIII (the infixed -t- between the first and second root letters), which here carries a reflexive sense of holding oneself back — 'to desist, restrain oneself'. The ya- prefix is the marker for 'he'; the nūn that follows it is the first letter of the root ن-ه-ي (not part of the person-marker), and the -t- is the Form VIII infix. Normally the verb would end in -ī (yantahī), but because the particle 'lam' before it forces the jussive mood, the ending is cut off to a bare -i (yantahi). The clipped ending is itself the grammatical sign that 'lam' is acting on it.
4.root: ن-ه-ي (n-h-y) — to forbid, to come to an end / desist

5.meaning: 'We shall surely seize and drag him violently' — to grab him and haul him forcibly. The 'We' is the royal/majestic plural of Allah, conveying power and certainty of the threat.
5.grammar: A present/future verb, first-person plural ('We'), made emphatic at both ends. The prefixed lām (la-) is the answer to the earlier oath/condition — it delivers the promised consequence ('then We will certainly…'). The na- prefix means 'We' (the majestic plural of Allah). The final -an is the light nūn of emphasis (nūn al-tawkīd al-khafīfa), a suffix that attaches to verbs to intensify them; in the Quranic text it is written in its pausal (waqf) form with an alif, which is why it looks like nunation but is not — true tanwīn is a noun ending and never occurs on a verb. The suffix doubles down on the certainty: 'We absolutely will drag him'. The verb itself means to grab the forelock and drag forcefully.
5.root: س-ف-ع (s-f-ʿ) — to seize/grip and drag, to strike or brand

6.meaning: 'By the forelock' — the hair at the very front of the head. To seize someone by the forelock is an image of total domination and humiliation: the person is utterly at the mercy of the one gripping them.
6.grammar: A noun with two prefixes. The prefixed bi- means 'by' or 'by means of' and shows the instrument or point of grabbing — it is what makes the dragging-verb take hold of something. The al- is 'the'. Because bi- is a preposition, the noun takes the genitive case, shown by the final -i (nāṣiyati). Note the assimilation: the 'l' of al- merges into the following 'n' (a 'sun letter'), so the whole is pronounced 'bin-nāṣiyati' — the bi- preposition stays and only the lām of 'al-' drops into the doubled nūn.
6.root: ن-ص-ي (n-ṣ-y) — the forelock / front of the head

1.meaning: A forelock — the lock of hair at the very front of the head, above the forehead. The previous verse warns that the defiant person will be seized and dragged by this forelock; here that forelock is named and then described. To grasp someone by the forelock is an image of total humiliation and complete seizure.
1.grammar: A singular feminine noun. It ends in taa marbuta (ة), the feminine marker, which is pronounced as -t- (nāṣiyat-) once a case vowel follows it. The final diacritic ٍ is tanwīn kasra, a single fused ending (-in): it marks the word as indefinite ('a forelock') and as genitive in one form — the two functions are not separable pieces stacked together. The word is genitive because it stands in apposition (badal) to the genitive noun 'forelock' in verse 15, taking on that word's case. Being indefinite and named on its own also lends a tone of contempt — merely 'a forelock.'
1.root: ن-ص-ي (n-ṣ-y) — the forelock / front lock of hair

2.meaning: Lying — given to falsehood, habitually untruthful. Although it grammatically describes the 'forelock,' the meaning points to the person himself: his speech and his claims are lies. Naming the forelock as 'lying' is a vivid way of pinning the lie onto the whole person.
2.grammar: An active participle (the doer of the verb 'to lie'), feminine to agree with the feminine noun 'forelock.' The long -ā- inside (kā-) is the participle pattern fāʿil(ah) meaning 'one who does' the action — so 'one that lies,' not just a single past lie. It ends in taa marbuta (ة), pronounced -t- (kādhibat-) before the case vowel. The final ٍ is tanwīn kasra (-in), the single indefinite-genitive ending, matching word 1: an adjective copies the case and indefiniteness of the noun it describes.

3.meaning: Sinful — wrongdoing, in error, guilty of offense against Allah. Like 'lying,' it describes the forelock but indicts the person: he is not merely mistaken but a deliberate wrongdoer. The pairing 'lying, sinful' joins false belief with evil deeds.
3.grammar: An active participle (the one who commits the action), feminine to agree with 'forelock.' The long -ā- (khā-) is the fāʿil(ah) 'one who does' pattern — a habitual or characteristic sinner, not a one-time slip. It ends in taa marbuta (ة), pronounced -t- (khāṭiʾat-) before the case vowel. The final ٍ is tanwīn kasra (-in), the single indefinite-genitive ending, matching words 1 and 2 and keeping all three in step as noun + two adjectives describing the same thing.

1.meaning: "So let him call (summon) [them]." A command-form verb meaning to call out to, summon, or appeal to someone for help. In context it is a challenge to the arrogant man (Abu Jahl): "Then let him go ahead and summon" his supporters — daring him to call on his allies, with the implication that they will be of no use against Allah.
1.grammar: Built from three pieces. The فَ (fa-) links this to the previous verse ("so/then…"). The لۡ (li-) is the "lām of command": placed on a present-tense verb it turns "he calls" into "let him call" — a third-person command. The يَ- prefix means "he." The command lām puts the verb in the jussive (command) mood, and it is that mood — not any change in spelling by itself — that signals "let him" rather than a plain statement. The morphological side-effect is visible here: the root ends in a weak wāw, so the plain form would be yadʿū with a long final "oo" (and a written wāw), but in the jussive that weak letter drops and the ending becomes a short "-u" (yadʿu).
1.root: د-ع-و (d-ʿ-w) — to call, summon, invoke, appeal to

2.meaning: "His council / his assembly" — the circle of people he could call upon: his clan, his supporters, the company that gathered with him. The word denotes the gathering or assembly itself, and by extension the people in it whom one would summon for backing. Here it points to the allies the arrogant man is dared to call for help.
2.grammar: Two pieces: the noun nādī ("assembly, council") plus the attached pronoun هٗ (-hu) meaning "his." This noun is "defective" (manqūs): its third root letter is a yāʾ that gets suppressed when the word stands alone and indefinite (it surfaces only as nunation, nādin). When a possessive pronoun is attached, that hidden yāʾ comes back as a real consonant, giving nādiya-hu ("his council"). The noun is also the object of the verb "call," so it is in the accusative — and the accusative fatḥa simply rides on that restored yāʾ as the "-iya-" sound; the "-a" you hear is the noun's own yāʾ becoming audible, not a separate case ending tacked on. So the form reads "summon his assembly" — i.e., let him call together the people on his side.
2.root: ن-د-و (n-d-w) — to call together, gather; an assembly / council (related to nadwah, a gathered council)

1.meaning: "We shall call / We will summon." A divine first-person-plural statement of what Allah will do: He will call out for — i.e. summon — the angelic guards of Hell. The 'we' here is the royal/majestic plural used of Allah, conveying might and authority, not number. The future marker frames this as a sure, impending consequence of the defiant person's behaviour described just before.
1.grammar: Present/future verb, first-person plural ('we'). The prefix sa- means the action is yet to happen ('will/shall'). The na- prefix is the 'we' subject built into the verb. The stem is from daʿā / yadʿū ('to call'). The verb is imperfect indicative (marfūʿ), and in recitation it keeps its full long final -ū (sanadʿū); the wāw is simply not written in the Uthmanic spelling (سَنَدۡعُ, not سَنَدۡعُو) — an orthographic convention, not a shortening of the vowel, and the sa- prefix has no effect on it. So the whole word already means a complete sentence: 'We will call.'

2.meaning: "The Zabāniyah" — the stern angelic wardens/enforcers of Hell who seize and drive the wicked into the Fire. There is no neat English word; they are the fierce angel-guards appointed over Hell's punishment. This word is the object of the previous verb: the ones Allah 'will call/summon.'
2.grammar: A definite noun ('the…'), here the direct object of the verb 'We will call.' The final -a (fatḥa) ending is the accusative case, which marks it as the thing acted upon — i.e. the ones being summoned. (The 'l' of al- is pronounced doubled into the following z- — 'az-zabāniyata' — because z is a 'sun letter.') It is a plural-in-meaning collective term for these angels.
2.root: ز-ب-ن (z-b-n) — to push away, repel, thrust; the classical lexicons derive al-Zabāniyah from this root, fitting these angels' role of thrusting the wicked into the Fire

1.meaning: A firm word of rebuke and deterrence — like saying 'No indeed!', 'Absolutely not!', or 'Stop right there!'. It both rejects the wrongdoer's behaviour described just before (the man who tried to stop the Prophet from praying) and braces the listener for the command that follows. There is no single English word for it; it is an emphatic 'never' that closes the door on the previous claim.
1.grammar: An indeclinable particle (it never changes its ending), so the final -ā is fixed and carries no case or tense. It functions as a standalone exclamation of rejection and warning, scolding what came before and signalling a sharp turn to the instruction ahead.

2.meaning: The word of prohibition 'do not'. Standing before the next verb, it forbids the action — turning 'you obey' into 'do not obey'. It is a command not to do something, addressed to the Prophet (peace be upon him).
2.grammar: This is the 'lā of prohibition' (lā an-nāhiya): a particle that issues a negative command. It forces the verb after it into the jussive mood, which is why the following verb loses its final vowel and ends in a silent stop (sukūn). It carries no ending of its own.

3.meaning: 'Obey him / comply with him / do as he says.' The 'him' refers to the defiant man (Abū Jahl) who tried to forbid the Prophet from praying. Combined with the preceding 'do not', the sense is: give him no compliance whatsoever.
3.grammar: A present-tense verb of Form IV (af'ala pattern: aṭāʿa, 'to obey'), put into the jussive by the preceding 'lā', so its ending is a silent stop (sukūn on the ʿ: tuṭiʿ) rather than a vowel — that clipped ending is what marks the prohibition. The tu- prefix marks 'you' (second person, masculine singular). The attached -hu is the object pronoun 'him'. Together with 'lā' it means 'do not obey him'.

4.meaning: 'But prostrate! / Rather, fall down in prostration (sujūd).' A direct command to place the forehead on the ground in worship of Allah — the posture of utmost humility and submission in prayer. The 'but/rather' contrasts it with the forbidden obedience: instead of yielding to the man, yield to Allah in prostration.
4.grammar: A prefix wa- ('and', here with the contrasting force of 'rather') joined to a command verb (imperative). The opening vowel is a 'helping' hamza (hamzat al-waṣl) that lets the word begin; the command itself is addressed to 'you' (masculine singular). It ends in a silent stop (sukūn: -jud), which is the normal ending for this kind of command. A prostration (sajda) is marked here in the text.
4.root: س-ج-د (s-j-d) — prostration, bowing the face to the ground

5.meaning: 'And draw near! / come close (to Allah).' A command to seek nearness to Allah — to close the distance between the servant and his Lord through worship and devotion. The object 'to Allah' is understood rather than spoken.
5.grammar: A prefix wa- ('and') joined to a command verb (imperative) of Form VIII (the ift-ʿala pattern, iqtaraba), which here adds a sense of actively bringing oneself close — 'draw your own self near'. The opening vowel is a 'helping' hamza (hamzat al-waṣl); the command is addressed to 'you' (masculine singular) and ends in a silent stop (sukūn: -rib), the standard ending for such a command.
